title: Angulimala stops
hook: a murderer wearing a necklace of fingers meets the Buddha, stops, and becomes a monk (Majjhima Nikaya 86)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was khima: where forgiveness is, there is God himself. Your line was God's own self, present there.

A road through a forest in the kingdom of Kosala, and the people along it are afraid. The sutta says villages and towns have been laid waste. A killer lives in those trees, and he wears a garland made of his victims' fingers. People call him Angulimala. One morning a monk walks down that road alone. Cowherds and farmers shout at him to turn around. He keeps walking, in silence. The monk is the Buddha.
screen: `AN EMPTY ROAD.` → `A GARLAND OF FINGERS.` → `A MONK WALKS IN ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Angulimala sees the monk coming, takes up his sword and shield, and runs after him. Then, in the sutta's telling, something strange happens: he runs as hard as he can and can't catch up with the Buddha, who is only walking at his usual pace. Out of breath, he shouts: stop, monk! The Buddha keeps walking and says, in paraphrase: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. Angulimala is baffled; the monk is plainly still walking. So the Buddha explains: he has stopped harming living beings, for good. Angulimala hasn't. Angulimala throws his weapons away into a chasm, bows at the Buddha's feet, and asks to become a monk. The Buddha says, come, monk, and that's his ordination. Later King Pasenadi rides out with soldiers to hunt the killer, and finds him sitting quietly in robes among the monks. The king is astonished. The sutta doesn't pretend it's easy. Walking for alms one day, Angulimala is hit by thrown stones and comes back bleeding, his bowl broken. The Buddha tells him to bear it: this is the fruit of what he did, ripening now. The change is real, and the past is real too; the sutta holds both. This is a case with blood on it, and the Buddha's first words to him were neither an excuse nor a sentence. They were: you stop too.
screen: `HE CAN'T CATCH A WALKING MONK.` · `I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO.` · `A KILLER IN ROBES.` · `STONES ON THE ALMS ROUND.` · then, large: `HE STOPPED.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've quietly written off as just like that and always will be, a relative, an old friend, a public figure, and hold their face for a moment. Without excusing anything they did, try one sentence in your mind: this person could stop. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words.
Angulimala stops. The killer who couldn't catch a walking monk, heard I have stopped, you stop too, and threw his weapons away. Today's word.
Your line: he stopped. Stopping came first; the robes came after. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell the story of Angulimala from the Majjhima Nikaya as a sign that even a killer can change, and some Buddhists chant verses from the same sutta, linked to Angulimala and a woman in labor, as a blessing for childbirth.

chat.says: What did the Buddha mean when he told Angulimala, 'I have stopped'?
options: He had stopped harming living beings for good, though he was still walking.
He meant he'd stopped walking and would wait there for Angulimala to come.
He meant he'd stopped teaching and wanted to be left alone on the road.
chat.meaning: In Majjhima Nikaya 86 the Buddha explains he has stopped harming living beings for good; Angulimala hasn't, yet.
